title: Cullen Skink
subtitle: Scottish smoked haddock and potato soup
excerpt: Smoked haddock poached in milk, then flaked into a thick soup with potato and onion. Scotland's most famous soup: smoky, rich, and deeply warming. Named after the village of Cullen in Moray.

recipe.sourceNotes: Cullen skink takes its name from the village of Cullen in Moray on the north-east coast of Scotland, where smoked haddock has been a staple for centuries. Skink is a Scots word for shin or knuckle of beef but was also applied to soups. The dish is now firmly established as Scotland's national soup. Finnan haddie, the traditional Aberdeenshire smoked haddock cure, is the authentic ingredient. Undyed smoked haddock is preferable to the bright yellow artificially dyed variety.

content.text: The flavour of this soup comes from poaching the haddock in the milk: the smoky juices infuse the milk and become the base of the soup. Use that milk, not fresh milk, to cook the potato. The soup should be thick and chunky, not smooth. Do not season with salt until after tasting: smoked haddock varies in saltiness.

Place the haddock in a wide saucepan. Cover with the milk and add the bay leaves. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 8 minutes. Remove the fish with a slotted spoon. Reserve the poaching milk, discarding the bay leaves. Flake the fish, discarding skin and any bones. Set aside.

Melt the butter in the same pan over medium heat. Fry the onion for 5 minutes until softened. Add the diced potato and the reserved poaching milk. Simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is completely tender.

Lightly mash some of the potato to thicken the soup, leaving plenty of chunks. Stir in the cream and flaked haddock. Heat gently without boiling. Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve with parsley and crusty bread.
